about: Simulator: a G protein-coupled receptor pathway (epinephrine, cAMP, PKA, a kinase cascade, glucose release). Model code: bio/assets/tools/bio-tool-math.js (ApBioMath.signal). Validator: scripts/lib/apbio-tool-checks/signal-transduction-amplification.mjs recomputes every number in the stimulus tables and the numeric answer, and checks the model's behavior (amplification at the enzyme steps, termination after washout, each block).
intro: Add epinephrine (adrenaline) to a liver cell and follow the signal from the receptor on the surface to the response inside: glucose units broken off glycogen. Count the active molecules at each step to see where the signal grows, wash the hormone away to watch the signal switch off, and block single steps with a drug or a toxin. Then answer the questions below about the same model.
howItWorks:
The pathway, one step at a time (each effect is the cause of the next):

  1. Reception. Epinephrine binds a G protein-coupled receptor. Binding is reversible: the fraction of receptors with epinephrine bound moves toward [L] / ([L] + Kd), with Kd = 10 nM (half of the receptors are bound at 10 nM). After washout, epinephrine leaves the receptors within a few seconds.
  2. G protein. A bound receptor changes shape and makes G proteins release GDP and pick up GTP, which switches them on. One receptor keeps doing this, about 10 G proteins per second, so this step amplifies. An active G protein switches itself off by hydrolyzing its GTP to GDP (on average after 4 seconds). A few G proteins switch on by themselves now and then.
  3. Adenylyl cyclase. An active G protein (its α subunit) binds and switches on one adenylyl cyclase. One-to-one binding passes the signal on but does not amplify it.
  4. cAMP. Each active adenylyl cyclase makes about 100 cAMP molecules per second from ATP (amplifies). Phosphodiesterase breaks cAMP down to AMP, 10% of the cAMP each second.
  5. PKA. cAMP binds protein kinase A (PKA) and frees its active (catalytic) parts. Several cAMP molecules are bound for each part freed, so this step uses cAMP up rather than multiplying it: active PKA = PKAtotal × C² / (C² + Kc²).
  6. Kinase cascade. Each active PKA phosphorylates about 1 phosphorylase kinase per second, and each active phosphorylase kinase phosphorylates about 2 glycogen phosphorylase molecules per second (both amplify). Phosphatases remove the phosphates, 20% of the active molecules each second.
  7. Response. Each active glycogen phosphorylase breaks about 10 glucose units off glycogen per second (amplifies).

The drugs and toxins (each acts from time 0):

  • Receptor antagonist: binds the receptor without activating it and competes with epinephrine. At the dose used, Kd behaves as if it were 21 times higher (210 nM), so more epinephrine can overcome it.
  • G protein locked on: the G protein cannot hydrolyze its GTP, so once it has GTP it stays active, with or without epinephrine. Cholera toxin does this to the stimulatory G protein of intestinal cells; the cAMP it raises opens chloride channels and water follows the ions out of the cells.
  • G protein locked off: the G protein cannot exchange GDP for GTP, so a bound receptor cannot switch it on. (Pertussis toxin locks a different, inhibitory G protein this way; the model applies the lock to the stimulatory one.)
  • Phosphodiesterase inhibitor: 90% less cAMP breakdown.
  • PKA inhibitor: blocks the active site of PKA. cAMP still binds PKA, but no target gets phosphorylated.

Simplifications: counts are molecules in one cell, with made-up but realistic proportions. The model takes steps of 0.05 s and starts from a resting cell. Real cells also switch receptors off after long exposure, have several kinds of G protein, and use PKA to switch off glycogen synthesis at the same time. Each trial you run adds random scatter (standard deviation 3%), like measurement error in a lab; the curves show the model without scatter.

gprotein.name: Locked on (cannot hydrolyze GTP, like cholera toxin)

sig-s1.title: Epinephrine signaling in a liver cell model
sig-s1.text: A student used the model. Table 1 shows the active molecules at each step 60 s after 10 nM epinephrine was added to a resting cell. In Table 2, epinephrine (10 nM) was added at 0 s and washed out at 120 s, with no drug, with a phosphodiesterase inhibitor, or with the G protein locked on. Table 3 shows the response 60 s after adding epinephrine at different concentrations, with and without a receptor antagonist.

tables.caption: Table 1. Active molecules per cell 60 s after adding 10 nM epinephrine
Table 2. Glucose release (millions of glucose units per second); epinephrine washed out at 120 s
Table 3. Glucose release (millions of glucose units per second) 60 s after adding epinephrine

questions.q: In Table 1 there are fewer active adenylyl cyclase molecules than active G proteins, yet about a thousand times more cAMP molecules than active adenylyl cyclase molecules. Which explanation is most consistent with the model?
options: Each active G protein switches on at most one adenylyl cyclase, but each active adenylyl cyclase keeps making cAMP from ATP
Adenylyl cyclase is destroyed after it makes one cAMP, so only a few active molecules are left at any moment
Each cAMP molecule is copied by the cell, so cAMP multiplies itself once it is made
Epinephrine binds adenylyl cyclase directly, and the G proteins only slow the signal down

why.correct: Binding one G protein to one cyclase passes the signal on without multiplying it, so the count does not grow at that step. An active cyclase is an enzyme that works again and again, so each one makes many cAMP molecules: that is where the signal is amplified.
options: Right: one-to-one binding does not amplify, while an enzyme that keeps working does.
An enzyme is not used up by the reaction it catalyzes; an active cyclase keeps making cAMP for as long as it stays bound to an active G protein.
cAMP is made by an enzyme from ATP; it does not copy itself.
Epinephrine binds the receptor on the cell surface. The receptor activates G proteins, and the G proteins activate the cyclase.

questions.q: Using Table 1, calculate the number of cAMP molecules in the cell for each receptor with epinephrine bound. Give a whole number.

why.correct: cAMP per bound receptor = 2,080,000 / 500 = 4,160. Each bound receptor activates many G proteins, and each active adenylyl cyclase makes many cAMP molecules, so one binding event leads to thousands of second messenger molecules.

questions.q: In Table 2, after washout the response with no drug falls almost to zero by 180 s, but with the phosphodiesterase inhibitor it stays high. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
options: Without breakdown of cAMP to AMP, cAMP stays high after the receptors are empty, so PKA and the kinases after it stay active
The inhibitor keeps epinephrine bound to the receptor after washout, so the receptor keeps activating G proteins
The inhibitor blocks the phosphatases, so the phosphorylated enzymes cannot be switched off
The inhibitor makes adenylyl cyclase work faster, so more cAMP is made after washout than before

why.correct: After washout the receptors empty and the G proteins switch off within seconds, so cAMP is no longer made. With working phosphodiesterase the remaining cAMP is broken down and the signal ends. With the enzyme blocked, the cAMP already made lingers, PKA stays active and the cascade keeps going.
options: Right: signal termination needs the second messenger removed, and the inhibitor stops its removal.
The inhibitor acts on phosphodiesterase inside the cell, not on the receptor; epinephrine still leaves the receptor after washout.
Phosphatases still work in the model; the cascade stays on because active PKA keeps re-phosphorylating its targets.
Adenylyl cyclase is switched off after washout because the G proteins hydrolyze their GTP; the cAMP left over is cAMP that is not broken down.

questions.q: Which claim about the receptor antagonist is best supported by Table 3?
options: It competes with epinephrine for the receptor, because raising the epinephrine concentration brings the response back close to the response without antagonist
It blocks a step after the receptor, because the response with antagonist stays near zero at every epinephrine concentration
It has no effect at low epinephrine concentrations and blocks the response only at high ones
It increases the response, because the response with antagonist keeps rising as epinephrine rises

why.correct: At 10 nM epinephrine the antagonist cuts the response from 3.40 to 0.40 million per second, but at 200 nM the response with antagonist (3.38) is almost as high as without it (3.84). More epinephrine wins more of the binding sites, which is what a competitor for the receptor shows.
options: Right: the antagonist's effect shrinks as epinephrine rises, so the two compete for the same binding site.
The response with antagonist reaches 3.38 million per second at 200 nM, so the steps after the receptor still work.
The antagonist has its largest effect at low concentrations (0.01 against 1.05 at 1 nM) and almost none at 200 nM.
The response rises with epinephrine in both columns; at every concentration it is lower with the antagonist than without it.

questions.q: The student repeats the experiment of Table 1 with a PKA inhibitor added at 0 s. Which prediction is most consistent with the model?
options: Bound receptors, active G proteins and cAMP are close to the values in Table 1, but almost no phosphorylase kinase or glycogen phosphorylase is active and glucose release stops
Every value in the table falls to nearly zero, because blocking any step stops the whole pathway
cAMP falls to nearly zero, because PKA is needed to make cAMP
Glucose release is unchanged, because the G proteins can activate glycogen phosphorylase directly

why.correct: The steps before PKA do not depend on PKA, so they run as before. With PKA blocked, phosphorylase kinase is not phosphorylated, glycogen phosphorylase stays inactive and no glucose is released: a block stops only the steps after it.
options: Right: the steps upstream of the block are unaffected, and everything downstream of it stops.
A block acts on the steps after it. Receptor binding, G protein activation and cAMP production happen before PKA.
Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP; PKA is activated by cAMP, not the other way around.
In this pathway the G protein acts through adenylyl cyclase and cAMP; it does not reach glycogen phosphorylase by any other route.

frq.title: Mini free-response question: amplifying and ending a signal

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe how the number of active molecules changes from bound receptors to glucose release per second in Table 1, and identify one step at which the signal is amplified.

rubric.point: Describes a large overall increase (from 500 bound receptors to about 3.4 million glucose units per second) AND identifies an amplifying step: bound receptor to G protein, adenylyl cyclase to cAMP, PKA to phosphorylase kinase, phosphorylase kinase to glycogen phosphorylase, or glycogen phosphorylase to glucose release.
accept: each active enzyme makes or activates many molecules of the next step
about 6,800 glucose units per second for each bound receptor

parts.sample: The numbers grow from 500 bound receptors to about 3,400,000 glucose units released per second, nearly 7,000 for each bound receptor. One amplifying step is adenylyl cyclase to cAMP: about 2,090 active cyclase molecules give 2,080,000 cAMP molecules.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain why glucose release falls almost to zero within 60 s of washout with no drug, but stays high with the phosphodiesterase inhibitor (Table 2).

rubric.point: Explains that after washout epinephrine leaves the receptors, the G proteins hydrolyze GTP (switch off) and adenylyl cyclase stops making cAMP.
accept: the signal is no longer received, so no new cAMP is made

rubric.point: Explains that phosphodiesterase normally breaks down the remaining cAMP (to AMP), so PKA and the cascade switch off (phosphatases undo the phosphorylations); with the inhibitor cAMP is not removed, so PKA stays active and glucose release continues.
accept: the second messenger lingers when its breakdown is blocked

parts.sample: When epinephrine is washed out, it leaves the receptors, the active G proteins hydrolyze their GTP to GDP and switch off, and adenylyl cyclase stops making cAMP. Phosphodiesterase then breaks the cAMP that is left down to AMP, PKA releases its targets, and phosphatases remove the phosphates from the kinases, so glucose release stops. With phosphodiesterase blocked, the cAMP already made is not broken down, so PKA stays active and the cascade keeps releasing glucose long after the hormone is gone.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Predict how adding the receptor antagonist would change glucose release in cells whose G protein is locked on, 60 s after adding 10 nM epinephrine. Justify your prediction.

rubric.point: Predicts that glucose release stays high (at most a little lower than without the antagonist, and far above the 0.40 million per second the antagonist allows in normal cells) AND justifies it: the antagonist only slows how fast G proteins are switched on, but locked-on G proteins never switch off, so they keep accumulating and keep adenylyl cyclase active.
accept: the block is upstream of a step that is stuck on
G proteins switched on by the few bound receptors, or on their own, stay on

parts.sample: Glucose release would stay high: perhaps a little lower at 60 s than without the antagonist, but far above the 0.40 million per second that the antagonist allows in normal cells (Table 3). The antagonist only reduces how many receptors are bound, and so how fast G proteins are switched on. A locked-on G protein never switches off, so the G proteins switched on by the few bound receptors keep piling up and keep adenylyl cyclase active. A block before a step that is stuck on has little lasting effect.
